result.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers plot every point correctly and label each fare. B uses a linear distance axis starting at $0 with titled axes on both sides. Its cap annotation is tied directly into the chart: a dashed flat line runs past 160 km with an inline label ('$21.00 for any longer trip'). A's log x-axis is honest and noted in the subtitle, but it has no y-axis title, its 'Fare cap' line sits at the chart edge and shows nothing beyond 160 km, and the tooltip, card styling and dark-mode code add some weight. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): A plots distance on a true linear scale. Its continuous line shows fares rising more slowly as distance grows. It labels both axes with units, and its dashed flat line past 160 km ties the cap note to the chart. B labels its log x-axis clearly, but the log scale makes the fare curve look like it speeds up, which works against its own claim that fares rise more slowly. B also has no y-axis title, and its tooltip, dark mode and hit-area code are extras the request didn't need.
